value.overview: The Snail Kite is a specialized wetland raptor that feeds mainly on freshwater snails. Its strongly curved bill is adapted for extracting snails from their shells. Adult males are dark gray, while females and young birds are brown and streaked. The species is broadly distributed from Florida and the Caribbean through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, local bird associated with suitable marshes, lakes, rivers, and seasonally flooded wetlands.
value.classification: The Snail Kite belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the order Accipitriformes. Its scientific name is Rostrhamus sociabilis.
value.identification: This medium-sized kite has broad wings, a short tail, and a distinctive white patch at the base of the tail. Adult males are slate gray to nearly black, with red eyes, an orange to reddish cere and legs, and a strongly hooked bill. Females and immature birds are brown with paler streaking on the head, neck, and underparts. In flight, it often shows slow, deep wingbeats and may circle low over marshes. Its specialized bill helps distinguish it from other Costa Rican kites.
value.rangeHabitat: The Snail Kite ranges from Florida, Cuba, and southern Mexico through parts of Central America and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it occurs locally and is generally uncommon, with records from wetland regions including the Tempisque Basin and Guanacaste marshes, as well as other lowland sites. It uses freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, flooded savannas, slow rivers, oxbow wetlands, and areas with emergent vegetation, especially where apple snails and perching sites are abundant.
value.migrationStatus: The Costa Rican population appears to include resident birds, while some individuals recorded on the Caribbean slope may be northern migrants. Occurrence is local and irregular outside the principal wetland areas.
value.breeding: Snail Kites usually nest near wetlands, often in low trees, shrubs, or emergent vegetation over or beside shallow water. They may breed singly or in loose colonies, depending on food availability and nesting habitat. Both adults participate in incubating the eggs and feeding the young. The species breeds in Central and South America, but reliable information on the frequency and distribution of breeding within Costa Rica is limited; documented Costa Rican records should therefore be interpreted as local rather than representative of the entire country.
value.dietFeeding: Freshwater snails, especially apple snails and related ampullariid mollusks, make up most of the diet. The kite typically searches from a perch or while flying slowly over shallow water, then captures a snail with its feet. It carries the prey to a favored perch, grips the shell with one foot, and uses its narrow, sharply curved bill to remove the edible animal. Small crabs, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic prey may occasionally be taken.
value.behavior: Snail Kites are often seen singly, in pairs, or in small groups around wetlands. They perch conspicuously on dead branches, shrubs, or other elevated structures near feeding areas. Their flight is usually slow and buoyant, with broad wings and relaxed wingbeats. Birds may patrol the edge of marsh vegetation before dropping toward the water. Because their movements are closely tied to water levels and snail abundance, local numbers can vary between seasons and years.

conservation.populationTrend: Globally stable overall, with some regional increases in the northern part of the range and localized declines where wetlands have been damaged. Population size across the full range is not well quantified.
